(CNN) -- The U.S. Coast Guard on Thursday is searching for two fishermen missing after a commercial fishing vessel went down in remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands about 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska. The fishing vessel Courageous helps search for missing men in waters off Alaska. Four of the boat's crew members were rescued and five bodies retrieved Wednesday near the Amchitka Pass, a strait that connects the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The names have been withheld pending the notification of families, a Coast Guard statement said. "What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the boat. He told The Associated Press, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive." The Seattle-based company told the AP the survivors were Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling. The search began at about 1 a.m. Wednesday when the Coast Guard received an emergency signal from the Katmai, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and nearly 20-foot waves. The signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device on the Katmai that reacts when it's touched or splashed with water, Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said.  Watch a "Deadliest Catch" captain talk about what may have happened on the rough seas » . At about that time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, sent an e-mail to the Coast Guard saying that it received a message from the Katmai that water was flooding its rear compartment. The message also said that the vessel had lost steering. The Coast Guard tried to e-mail the Balard back but received no response, likely because the seas are remote and Internet access can be spotty, Read said. Rescuers launched a C-130, a long-range surveillance aircraft, and went straight to the scene twice Wednesday morning, Read said. The boat was nowhere in sight, but the C-130 did spot two strobe lights on top of the water, he said. By this time, the weather was treacherous and the sky was darkening, according to Read. The C-130, having found no signs of life, dropped two life rafts and headed back, he said. On the second trip, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter found two strobe lights floating in the water, one attached to a survival suit and the other to the emergency device that had first alerted the Coast Guard, Read said. They also found a body, he said. "We knew the person was from the Katmai because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said. Roughly five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four men on a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of other vessels, the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, the bodies of four other men were recovered from the water, all wearing survival suits, Read said. The odds of someone surviving the frigid waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands is minimal, said Read. Crews usually have survival suits that allow water to seep inside but have a mechanism that traps body heat. The search for the two remaining men began at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, an hour before sunrise there. "You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It's darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there."

# Cold Waters: The Sinking of the *Northern Venture* in the Bering Sea

*A journalistic reconstruction*

---

**Editor's note:** The following is a fictional journalistic account created for illustrative purposes. The vessel, individuals, and specific events described are invented, though the scenario draws on the real and well-documented dangers faced by commercial fishermen in Alaskan waters.

---

## A Routine Voyage Turns to Catastrophe

The *Northern Venture*, an 84-foot steel-hulled crabbing vessel out of Dutch Harbor, was three days into an opilio crab season run when disaster struck in the early hours of February 14th. The boat had been working the fishing grounds roughly 140 nautical miles northwest of St. Paul Island, in a stretch of the Bering Sea notorious for sudden weather and towering seas.

Captain Raymond "Ray" Delacroix, 52, a veteran of more than two decades in the fishery, had been monitoring a deepening low-pressure system on his weather routing software. What forecasts had described as 25-foot seas built rapidly to 35 feet, with winds gusting past 60 knots.

## The Failure

According to survivor accounts, the vessel began taking on water shortly after 2:00 a.m. Investigators would later focus on a failed lazarette hatch and possible icing that had accumulated on the deck and rigging, raising the boat's center of gravity and compromising its stability—a condition fishermen grimly call "getting top-heavy."

"We were fighting the ice all night, out there with baseball bats and mallets knocking it off the rails," recalled deckhand Marcus Two Rivers, 29. "But the water was coming in faster than the pumps could push it out."

By 2:40 a.m., the engine room had flooded, cutting main power. The vessel began to list severely to starboard.

## Alerting the Coast Guard

At 2:47 a.m., Captain Delacroix issued a **Mayday** over VHF Channel 16 and activated the vessel's **EPIRB** (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon). The distress signal was relayed via the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system to the Coast Guard's **17th District command center in Juneau**, which pinpointed the vessel's coordinates within minutes.

"The EPIRB is the single most important piece of equipment on a boat in that moment," said a Coast Guard spokesperson. "It tells us exactly where to look in an ocean where a person is invisible from a mile away."

Coast Guard Sector Anchorage immediately launched an **MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter** from Air Station Kodiak, with a **C-130 Hercules** aircraft dispatched to serve as an airborne communications relay and to drop supplies if needed. Because of the extreme distance, the helicopter required a mid-mission refueling stop at a forward staging point on St. Paul Island.

The cutter ***Alex Haley***, operating in the region, was also diverted toward the scene, though it was hours away.

## Abandoning Ship

With the *Northern Venture* rolling onto its side, the crew of six deployed a life raft and donned their neoprene survival suits—often called "Gumby suits"—at approximately 3:05 a.m.

"You practice the drills, but nothing prepares you for jumping into black water in the middle of the night," said Two Rivers. "The cold hits you like a wall. You can't breathe. All you can think about is your hands still working."

One crew member, engineer **Danny Kowalski, 41**, was swept from the deck before reaching the raft. Two shipmates managed to pull him back, an act that likely saved his life.

## The Rescue Timeline

- **2:47 a.m.** — Mayday and EPIRB activation
- **2:52 a.m.** — 17th District confirms distress position
- **3:05 a.m.** — Crew abandons ship into life raft
- **3:14 a.m.** — MH-60 Jayhawk launches from Kodiak
- **4:30 a.m.** — C-130 arrives on scene, establishes communications, drops flares to mark position
- **5:50 a.m.** — Jayhawk arrives after refueling; begins hoist operations
- **6:40 a.m.** — Final survivor recovered

The rescue swimmer, deployed into 38-degree water and 35-foot swells, brought survivors one at a time to the rescue basket. In seas that size, the helicopter must hover with precise timing to avoid the crests.

## The Survivors

Five of the six crew members survived:

- **Captain Raymond Delacroix**, 52 — Kodiak, Alaska
- **Marcus Two Rivers**, 29 — Bethel, Alaska
- **Danny Kowalski**, 41 — Seattle, Washington
- **Elena Vasquez**, 34 — Portland, Oregon (the vessel's only female crew member, a second-season deckhand)
- **Tommy Nguyen**, 26 — Dutch Harbor, Alaska

Deckhand **Samuel "Sam" Bright, 38**, of Anacortes, Washington, did not survive. He had become separated from the raft during the chaotic evacuation. His body was recovered later that morning by the *Alex Haley*.

## The Brutal Mathematics of Cold

Survival experts note that in water near freezing, an unprotected person can lose meaningful use of their limbs within minutes and lose consciousness within an hour. The crew's survival suits were the decisive factor.

"Those suits bought them the time the Coast Guard needed," said a maritime safety instructor familiar with the case. "Without them, this is a story with no survivors at all. The margin out there is measured in minutes."

The remoteness compounds every danger. Unlike coastal waters, the central Bering Sea offers no nearby harbor, no quick helicopter transit, and often no other vessels within reach. Rescuers work at the very edge of their aircraft's fuel range.

## Aftermath

The five survivors were transported to St. Paul Island, then flown to Anchorage for treatment of hypothermia and, in Kowalski's case, frostbite to his hands. All were released within days.

The **National Transportation Safety Board** and Coast Guard opened a joint investigation focused on vessel stability, ice accumulation, and the condition of the lazarette hatch. Findings from such investigations frequently reshape safety regulations across the fleet.

For the families of the *Northern Venture*, and for the tight-knit fishing community of Dutch Harbor, the loss was a stark reminder of what the industry demands. The Bering Sea remains one of the deadliest workplaces on Earth—and the men and women who fish it know the water gives no guarantees.

# Fishing Vessel Sinks in Bering Sea Storm; 2 Crew Members Still Missing

**By CNN Staff**

At least three crew members are dead and two remain missing after a commercial fishing vessel sank in the treacherous waters of the Bering Sea early Thursday, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

The 128-foot fishing vessel *Nordic Venture* went down roughly 180 miles southwest of St. Paul Island as a powerful winter storm battered the region with hurricane-force winds and towering seas, according to Coast Guard officials.

Of the 11 crew members aboard, six were rescued, three were recovered but did not survive, and two remain unaccounted for, the Coast Guard said in a statement.

## A Race Against Deadly Conditions

The Coast Guard said it received a distress signal from the vessel's emergency beacon at approximately 3:20 a.m. local time. A rescue helicopter and a C-130 aircraft were immediately dispatched from Air Station Kodiak, while the Coast Guard Cutter *Munro* diverted to the scene.

"Our crews were battling 40-mile-per-hour winds and seas of 25 to 30 feet," said Capt. Andrea Whitman, a Coast Guard spokesperson overseeing the response. "These are some of the most unforgiving conditions our rescue swimmers ever face. The survivors owe their lives to the fact that several of them made it into a life raft."

Whitman said water temperatures hovering near freezing left crew members with a narrow window for survival, making the rapid response critical.

The six survivors were hoisted from the life raft and a partially submerged section of the vessel before being transported to a medical facility in Anchorage. Two are being treated for hypothermia and are listed in stable condition, officials said.

## Search Continues for Missing Crew

The Coast Guard said search efforts for the two missing crew members were ongoing Thursday evening, though deteriorating weather threatened to hamper operations.

"We have not given up hope, and we will continue searching as long as conditions allow us to safely do so," Whitman said. "Our thoughts are with the families waiting for news."

## Company Responds

The vessel is owned by Arctic Bering Seafoods, a Seattle-based commercial fishing company. In a statement Thursday afternoon, company spokesperson Michael Doyle expressed grief over the loss.

"Our entire company is heartbroken by this tragedy," Doyle said. "The men and women aboard the *Nordic Venture* are part of our family. We are doing everything in our power to support the survivors, the families of those we've lost, and the crews still hoping for word on our missing colleagues."

Doyle said the company was cooperating fully with the Coast Guard and would participate in the investigation into what caused the vessel to sink.

## Among the World's Deadliest Waters

The Bering Sea remains one of the most dangerous places in the world to work, with commercial fishing consistently ranking among the deadliest occupations in the United States. Sudden storms, frigid temperatures and remote conditions leave little margin for error when disaster strikes.

The cause of the sinking has not been determined. The Coast Guard said an investigation would be launched once search-and-rescue operations conclude.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

The alarm was raised when watchstanders at the Coast Guard's regional command center received an activated Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) transmitting from the vessel's last known coordinates. ## Air and Sea Search Underway

Within hours of the alert, the Coast Guard deployed a C-130 Hercules fixed-wing aircraft from Air Station Kodiak to conduct an aerial search across the debris field and surrounding waters. The exact number of crew aboard the vessel and the cause of the sinking have not yet been confirmed. Investigators are expected to examine weather conditions, vessel integrity, and other factors once the immediate rescue phase concludes.
